title: Efficient Adaptive Data Acquisition via Pretrained Belief Representations
claim: A pretrained foundation model supplies belief representations to a lightweight policy head, which is trained with task-specific utilities and deployed in one forward pass.
layout: 3 panels: left architecture, right training and deployment stacked, dashed POLAR module boxes
description: The figure has a large left panel and two stacked panels on the right. The left panel shows the POLAR architecture bottom-up. A Tabular Foundation Model box holds sample attention, feature attention and MLP blocks, with the note 'Pretrained on diverse priors' and icons for random functions, random graphs and tree ensembles. An arrow leads up to a strip of green belief embeddings. A green Policy head box sits on top of the embeddings, joined by a plus sign. The top-right Training stage panel is a loop: simulated rollouts, then task-specific utility (BED, BO, AL pills), then policy loss, which updates the policy head. A dashed arrow for an optional prediction loss updates the backbone. The bottom-right Deployment stage panel is a cycle: next design, experiment, outcome, history, back to the POLAR policy head and backbone. Navy arrows, rounded boxes and pale grey, green and blue fills are used throughout.
caption: Overview of \method. Left: \method uses a pretrained tabular foundation model as a belief encoder and trains a policy head on top of it. Top right: Policy learning is driven by task-specific utilities, while backbone adaptation is supervised by an optional prediction loss. Bottom right: At deployment, the policy maps the current history to the next design in a single forward pass.
abstract: Learning effective policies for adaptive data acquisition remains challenging: posterior-based methods rely on surrogate models and posterior approximations that can be misspecified or biased, while direct policy-learning methods map from historical observations and fail to exploit available model representations, making learning harder. We introduce policy learning with belief representations (POLAR), based on the insight that optimal data acquisition depends on the observation history only through a sufficient belief state. Specifically, POLAR decouples representation learning from policy learning by leveraging pretrained predictive foundation models as belief-state encoders, training a policy head on top of their representations. This yields a simple, unified amortised policy learning framework for Bayesian experimental design, Bayesian optimisation, and active learning, differing only in the task-specific utility used to train the policy. Empirically, we find that POLAR outperforms state-of-the-art amortised methods across diverse tasks while requiring far fewer training samples, demonstrating a significant step in the scalability and efficiency of amortised data acquisition.
